brief: This week the hot startups list grew to 50 companies, with 22 new names joining for the first time. The strongest newcomer is Lovable, a Swedish startup that lets anyone describe an app in plain English and have its AI write the code and put it online, turning a technical breakthrough into something any ordinary person can use. The trend of the week is AI agents that do the work, not just chat, as startups like Lovable, Factory, n8n and Yoom sell agents that carry out whole jobs end to end instead of just answering questions.
gaps: Latin America is nearly invisible in this batch, with only Ontop (Colombia) representing the whole region through global payroll; nobody is pointing the molecule/material-design playbook of AQEMIA, Cradle and CuspAI, or the clinical-documentation playbook of Nabla and Tandem Health, at Latin America's huge agriculture or healthcare markets.

Elder care has no entry at all, even though Evvy shows a founder can win by targeting an underinvested health niche and Maven Robotics shows a wheeled arm-robot can be built for one ugly job; nobody has built the equivalent AI monitoring, companionship or robotics product for aging-in-place seniors.

Skilled trades and independent tradespeople (electricians, plumbers, HVAC techs) are only touched at the edges, through FYLD's construction field-data capture and Sona/Stream's frontline-worker pay tools; nobody offers the direct matching-and-dispatch layer that Jack & Jill built for white-collar job seekers or Maven Robotics built for warehouse labor.

Everyday mental health support is a gap: Loora proves people will hold real practice conversations with an AI tutor, and ElevenLabs/Synthflow show voice agents are now trusted for sales and tutoring calls, but nobody in this list has aimed that same conversational-voice technology at day-to-day mental health coaching or therapy support.

Sub-Saharan Africa is missing from the fintech and health-diagnostics wave; the MEA entries (barq in Saudi Arabia, Tarabut in Bahrain, Zeal in Egypt) cluster around the Gulf and North Africa, leaving open the same regulated-wallet or at-home-diagnostics model (as Evvy runs for women's health) for markets like Nigeria or Kenya.
run_line: 63 searches of 250, 108 pages of 200, 48 startups judged of 60, 97 minutes
title: Hot Startups

trends.name: AI voice agents
trends.sentence: Now that synthetic speech is good enough to trust, startups are putting AI voice agents directly into phone calls, sales conversations and even tutoring sessions.

trends.name: Space hardware for the new space economy
trends.sentence: Space startups are building the physical backbone of the sector, from reusable capsules and laser comms terminals to small and swarm satellites, sold mainly to governments and commercial operators.

trends.name: Self-fixing security and compliance
trends.sentence: Security and compliance tools are moving from just flagging problems to acting on their own, patching vulnerabilities, blocking attacks and running audits automatically.

trends.name: AI agents that do the work, not just chat
trends.sentence: A wave of startups sell AI agents that carry out whole jobs end to end, turning plain English into working apps, code fixes or office workflows instead of just answering questions.

trends.name: AI drafts clinical documentation
trends.sentence: AI is being trained to listen in on or read medical encounters, from doctor visits to X-rays, and automatically draft the clinical notes so clinicians spend less time on paperwork.

trends.name: Generative AI for molecules and materials
trends.sentence: Generative AI paired with physics or lab data is being used to design new drug molecules, proteins and materials, shortcutting years of trial-and-error lab work.
